abstract.p: Bispecific CD40 agonists could address biological and medical needs within immuno-oncology. The authors show that ATOR-4066, a CD40 and CEACAM5 bispecific antibody, effectively targets myeloid cells in tumors and enhances the antitumor activity of tumor-specific T cells.

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Despite recent progress within the field of immuno-oncology, immune suppression in the tumor microenvironment, defective antigen presentation, and low levels of tumor-specific T cells are key limitations of current cancer immunotherapies. CD40-targeting immunotherapies hold promise for addressing these limitations across solid tumors. In this study, we describe ATOR-4066, a bispecific antibody that targets CD40 and CEACAM5, developed using the Neo-X-Prime platform. ATOR-4066 showed potent CEACAM5-dependent activation in vitro, with an ability to activate intratumoral immune cells from patient-derived material. In vivo, ATOR-4066 induced superior antitumor activity compared with a CD40 mAb in MC38–carcinoembryonic antigen tumors and cured mice with well-established tumors with heterogeneous CEACAM5 expression. Using RNA sequencing, flow cytometry, and cytokine analysis, we showed that ATOR-4066 promoted immune cell trafficking to tumors and activated both myeloid cells and T cells within the tumor microenvironment, with limited immune activation in the periphery. ATOR-4066 initially induced a T cell–independent antitumor response, yet we found that a functional T-cell response was critical for long-term tumor control and immunity directed to tumor antigens other than CEACAM5. Finally, we demonstrated that ATOR-4066 synergized with PD-1 blockade in vitro. In conclusion, these data provide mechanistic evidence for the proposed mode of action and support further development of ATOR-4066 in CEACAM5-expressing cancers.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Although the advent of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) has profoundly transformed cancer therapy, the efficacy of ICI therapy relies on the presence of an existing immune response within the tumor microenvironment (TME). Tumors that lack sufficient immune cell infiltration remain a substantial unmet clinical need (1, 2). Furthermore, many tumors are heavily infiltrated with suppressive immune cells that dampen the immune response in the TME and prevent the activity of standard-of-care chemotherapies (2). CD40-targeting therapies provide an opportunity to address these challenges and may offer new treatment paradigms in multiple solid tumors (3, 4).

CD40 (also known as TNFRSF5) is a member of the TNF receptor superfamily that is expressed on the surface of antigen-presenting cells (APC), including dendritic cells (DC), B cells, and macrophages, as well as on other cell types such as epithelial, endothelial, and neoplastic cells (5). Signaling through CD40 promotes the ability of DCs to induce tumor-specific T-cell responses, and therapies targeting CD40 have emerged as a promising strategy to overcome resistance to ICIs (6, 7). CD40-targeting therapies aimed at augmenting the priming of tumor-specific T cells have the potential to increase response rates in indications in which ICI therapies are approved but have limited activity, as well as to expand the scope of eligible immunotherapy indications by making tumors more inflamed (8, 9). Additionally, CD40 signaling in macrophages can alleviate the immunosuppressive TME and remodel the extracellular matrix, sensitizing a tumor to standard-of-care chemotherapies (3, 10). Clinical evidence supporting the benefits of agonistic CD40 antibodies in combination with chemotherapy is emerging (11).

Bispecific antibody (bsAb) formats provide new opportunities to target CD40 to enhance antitumor immune responses and direct the immune activation to the TME, thereby increasing efficacy and reducing the risk of toxicities induced by systemic immune activation (6). Several bispecific therapies binding CD40 and a second target are under development to explore this potential. We have previously described the Neo-X-Prime platform of bispecific CD40 antibodies designed to engage both CD40 and tumor-associated antigens (TAA) to enhance antitumor efficacy while maintaining a good tolerability profile (12). Preclinical studies demonstrated that bispecific CD40 antibodies developed within the Neo-X-Prime platform induce superior T-cell cross-priming compared with monospecific CD40 agonists and that this translates into improved antitumor activity compared with combinations of CD40- and TAA-monotargeting compounds (12).

CEACAM5 is a 180 kDa glycosyl phosphatidyl inositol (GPI)-linked glycoprotein belonging to the carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA)–related cell adhesion superfamily and is involved in cell adhesion and migration (13). CEACAM5 is overexpressed in carcinomas of the gastrointestinal tract, the genitourinary and respiratory systems, and breast cancer (14). However, CEACAM5 has limited expression in normal adult tissue (13), in which it is mainly expressed in a polar manner on the apical surface of colon epithelial cells, making it inaccessible for systemically administered CEACAM5-targeting antibodies (15, 16). In tumors, the loss of polarization of malignant cells results in an abnormal distribution of CEACAM5 on the cell surface, making it accessible to systemically administered antibodies. This also increases the shedding of CEACAM5, resulting in increased serum levels of soluble CEACAM5 (13, 15, 17). Multiple CEACAM5-targeting strategies, including CEACAM5-targeting mAbs, antibody–drug conjugates (ADC), T-cell engagers, and chimeric antigen receptor T cells, have been pursued in the clinic (13, 15, 17).

ATOR-4066 is a bsAb developed from the Neo-X-Prime platform that targets CD40 and CEACAM5. The CD40-binding domain is derived from the CD40-binding domain of the monospecific mitazalimab antibody, which has demonstrated an excellent functional, safety, and immunogenicity profile in clinical studies (11, 18, 19). The selection of CEACAM5 as the targeting TAA for ATOR-4066 was based on its nonpolarized overexpression in tumors and its presence on tumor-derived extracellular vesicles and exosomes (20, 21). The latter aspect of CEACAM5 is critical for the mode of action of ATOR-4066, as it is designed to both increase the uptake of CEACAM5-expressing tumor-derived debris, exosomes, or other extracellular vesicles carrying tumor neoantigens by APCs to promote efficient cross-priming of neoantigen-specific T cells and to conditionally activate CD40-expressing cells in the TME (6, 12). Hägerbrand and colleagues demonstrated that ATOR-4066 (there referred to as CD40xCEA#1) induces the clustering of CEACAM5-positive tumor-derived extracellular vesicles with CD40-expressing APCs (12). Furthermore, it was demonstrated that ATOR-4066 induced CEACAM5-conditional agonistic activity of CD40-expressing cells in the presence of tumor cells with CEACAM5 densities expected on tumor cells but not on normal cells. Finally, a cynomolgus cross-reactive CD40xCEACAM5 bsAb was shown to be well tolerated in nonhuman primates in a pilot toxicology study (12).

In this study, we describe the key design features of ATOR-4066 and the treatment-induced changes in the immune system that correlate with the antitumor response. We found that ATOR-4066 activated both myeloid cells and T cells in the TME and increased monocyte and neutrophil infiltration into the tumor. ATOR-4066 initially induced a T cell–independent antitumor response, but a functional T-cell response was found to be critical for the eradication of tumors and long-term tumor immunity. Finally, we demonstrate that ATOR-4066 was able to enhance antitumor activity and immune activation driven by a PD-1 inhibitor.

sec.title: Antibodies and reagents
sec.p: The CEACAM5-targeting binding domain was isolated from Alligator’s proprietary antibody library, and the CD40 binder was developed using Alligator’s FIND technology (22). The bsAb ATOR-4066 targeting CD40xCEACAM5 was generated in the bispecific tetravalent RUBY format (patent no. WO 2023/079102; seqID nos. 29, 17, 130, 138; ref. 23). The Fc domain used for ATOR-4066 was IgG1 with LALA Fc attenuating mutations (23). A monospecific CD40 mAb containing the same CD40-binding domains as ATOR-4066 but with a wild-type (WT) IgG1 Fc domain (CD40 mAb; patent no. WO 2023/079102; seqID nos. 29, 17), a bsAb in the RUBY IgG1 LALA format with a high-affinity CEACAM5 binder targeting the same epitope as ATOR-4066 (CD40xCEACAM5 bsAb #3), and a bsAb with two irrelevant binders specific for GFP and human epithelial cell adhesion molecule (targets that are not present in any of the assays or models) that is herein named isotype bsAb (patent no. WO 2020/127376; seqID nos. 29, 31, 30, 32) served as control antibodies. Antibodies were produced transiently in Expi293 (Life Technologies), as previously described (12), or from stable Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) production cell lines generated using the glutamine synthetase–deficient CHOZn–glutamine synthetase (GS) cell platform, as previously described (22). Fed-batch cultivations were conducted in either shaker flasks (0.05 L or 1.0 L wvol) in-house or in 2 L (wvol) glass bioreactors (Univessel, Sartorius) at a contract manufacturing organization (CMO) facility. Bioreactors were maintained at pH 7.0 ± 0.1 and 50% dissolved oxygen. Inoculum density was 0.5 million viable cells/mL in HyClone ActiPro medium (SH31039.01, Cytiva). Fed-batch feeding was performed with Cell Boost 7 A/B (3% A and 0.3% B per day for 6 days; SH31119.01 and SH31120.01, Cytiva). Glucose levels were controlled at 6 g/L. Cultivations were carried out at 36.0°C with 8% (or 5%) CO2. Temperature was shifted to 35.0°C on day 5°C and 33.5°C on day 7. The process duration was 14 days. Purification from supernatants was made on protein A using the NGC system (Bio-Rad), the ÄKTA avant system (GE Healthcare), or PreDictor MabSelect SuRe (GE Healthcare). IgG titer was measured by high-performance liquid chromatography(protein A). All antibodies were quality controlled as described previously (23).

A list of antibodies used in this study is provided in Supplementary Table S1. Fixable Viability Stain 620 or Fixable Viability Stain 780 (564996 and 565388, BD Biosciences) was used to exclude dead cells from the analyses.

sec.title: Cell lines
sec.p: CHO (85051005, European Collection of Animal Cell Cultures) cells were cultured in RPMI 1640 supplemented with 10% FBS (SH30070.01, Cytiva) and 10 mmol/L 4-(2-hydroxyethyl)-1-piperazineethanesulfonic acid (15630-056, Gibco). MKN-45 cells (ACC 409, DSMZ) were cultured in RPMI 1640 supplemented with 20% FBS. MC38 cells (ENH204-FP, Kerafast) were cultured in DMEM with GlutaMAX (131966, Gibco) supplemented with 10% FBS, 1× nonessential amino acids (11140-050, Gibco; ref. 24), and 1 mmol/L sodium pyruvate (S8636-100, Sigma-Aldrich). MC38 cells transfected with human CEACAM5 were obtained from Kerafast (MC-38-CEA-2, ENH202-FP) and cultured as MC38 cells with the addition of 300 µg/mL geneticin (10131-027, Gibco; ref. 24). B16-F10 cells (CRL-6475, ATCC) were cultured in DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS.

CHO cells were transfected with human CEACAM5 in a pcDNA3.1 expression vector or an empty pcDNA3.1 expression vector using Lipofectamine LTX transfection reagents (A12621, Thermo Fisher Scientific), according to the manufacturer’s instructions, to generate CHO-CEACAM5 or control cells. Transfected cells were selected using 0.6 mg/mL geneticin (10131-027, Gibco). From the MC-38-CEA-2 cells, single-cell clones with high expression of CEACAM5 were selected and will be referred to herein as MC38-CEA. Receptor quantification of CEACAM5 on the MC38-CEA tumor cell line was performed using the Quantum Simply Cellular mouse kit (Bangs Laboratories 815B) according to the manufacturer’s instructions, using a CD66abce-APC antibody (130-118-539, Miltenyi Biotec, RRID: AB_2660529).

All cell lines were tested for Mycoplasma using the MycoAlert Mycoplasma Detection Kit (LT07-418, Lonza Bioscience). For in vitro assays, all cells were cultured for less than 20 passages. For in vivo experiments, cells were thawed and passaged 3 times before inoculation.

sec.title: Kinetic measurements
sec.p: CEACAM5 affinity of ATOR-4066 and control CD40xCEACAM5 bsAb #3 was determined using the Octet RED96 platform (Sartorius). ATOR-4066 or the control CD40-CEACAM5 bsAb #3 was coupled to anti-Human IgG Fc Capture biosensor tips (Sartorius) and assayed against 1:2 serially diluted monomeric CEACAM5 (4128-CM, R&D Systems), starting at 100 nmol/L. Binding kinetics was studied in 1× kinetic buffer (18-1105, Sartorius), in which association was allowed for 100 seconds, followed by dissociation for 100 seconds. Generated data were referenced by subtracting the blank or parallel buffer blank, the baseline was aligned to the y-axis, interstep correction by alignment against dissociation was performed, and the data were smoothed by the Savitzky–Golay filter in the data analysis software (v9.0.0.14). The processed data were fitted using a 1:1 Langmuir binding model.

sec.title: In vitro assays
sec.p: Human primary peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) were isolated from leukocyte concentrates obtained from healthy donors, with written consent, from Clinical Immunology and Transfusion Medicine (anonymized material, approved by the regional board at clinical transfusion medicine, approval nos. 2023:08 and 2024:13), Labmedicin Region Skåne. The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Human CD14+ monocytes were enriched from the PBMC by positive selection using MACS CD14 MicroBeads (130-050-201, Miltenyi Biotec). Monocyte-derived DCs (MoDC) were generated by differentiating the CD14+ monocytes for 1 week in Mo-DC Differentiation Medium supplemented with GM-CSF and IL-4 (130-094-812, Miltenyi Biotec). After 3 and 6 days, new media were added. On day 7, mature MoDCs were harvested for assay setup. On day 6, MKN-45 cells were sublethally irradiated using a UVB cross-linker (Analytik Jena, lamp: 254 nm) prior to being plated in 96-well plates overnight (5 × 104 tumor cells/well). The following day, on day 7, plates were centrifuged before serial dilutions of ATOR-4066 were added and incubated with MKN-45 tumor cells at 37°C for 30 minutes, followed by the addition of 5 × 104 matured MoDCs. On day 9, after 48 hours of incubation in a humid chamber at 37°C and 5% CO2, supernatant was harvested, and IL12 levels were measured by ELISA using a human IL12/IL23 (p40) ELISA development kit (3450-1A-6, Mabtech). IL12 levels from each donor were normalized between 0% and 100%, dose–response curves were plotted, and EC50 values were determined by nonlinear fit, agonist versus response variable slope (four parameters) using GraphPad Prism 9.3.1 (GraphPad Software, RRID: SCR_002798).

A CD40 reporter system (Promega, CD40 Bioassay Kit CS JA2155) or a primary B-cell assay was used to assess the impact of soluble CEACAM5 on ATOR-4066 function. In brief, CD40 reporter cells and ATOR-4066 or control bsAb (CD40xCEA bsAb #3) were added to the assay plates before the addition of CEACAM5-transfected CHO cells in the presence or absence of soluble CEACAM5 (0.5, 1, or 5 μg/mL, 4128-CM, R&D Systems). The assay plates were incubated for 6 hours at 37°C until the addition of Bio-Glo Luciferase Assay Detection solution and analyzed in a BMG ELISA plate reader. For the B-cell assay, B cells were enriched from PBMCs isolated from leukocyte concentrates obtained from healthy donors using the B Cell Isolation Kit II, human (130-091-151, Miltenyi Biotec). B cells (50,000 cells/well) were incubated with IL4 (10 ng/mL, 200-04, Gibco) in 96-well plates together with CHO-CEACAM5 cells (60,000 cells/well), CHO-WT cells (60,000 cells/well), soluble CEACAM5 (1 or 5 µg/mL), or the combination of CHO-CEACAM5 and soluble CEACAM5, with or without ATOR-4066 (1 nmol/L). After 48 hours, the cells were stained for viability (FVS780, 565388, BD Biosciences), and the expression of CD45, CD19, and CD86 (Supplementary Table S1) was analyzed by flow cytometry (BD FACSCanto II, BD Biosciences).

Domain mapping of the CD40 binder was performed by assessing binding to human CD40 receptors transfected into cells, in which domains or parts of domains (modules A and B of domain 1) have been replaced with the corresponding murine CD40 sequence as described by Ellmark and colleagues (25).

In vitro activation using patient-derived dissociated tumor cells (DTC) from six CEACAM5-positive gastric cancer tumors was analyzed for their ability to activate tumor-infiltrating immune cells following stimulation with ATOR-4066 for 72 hours. DTCs from patients with gastric cancer were purchased from Discovery Life Sciences. Directly after thawing, DTCs were counted using a NucleoCounter NC-200 (ChemoMetec), stained for CEACAM5 and CD40, and analyzed by flow cytometry to confirm target expression at baseline. Up to 200,000 viable gastric sample cells, containing both CD40-expressing immune cells and CEACAM5-expressing tumor cells, were seeded into a Nunc UpCell 96-well plate (174897, Thermo Fisher Scientific). Serial dilutions of ATOR-4066 were added to the wells. The plate was incubated for 3 days in a 37°C, 5% CO2 incubator. Next, the cells were harvested, stained for different cell surface markers, and analyzed by flow cytometry (FACSymphony A1, BD Biosciences) for the expression of the activation marker CD25 on CD8+ or CD4+ T cells or CD83 on CD19+ B cells or CD11b+ myeloid cells. For a list of antibody panels used for flow cytometry, see Supplementary Table S1.

sec.title: In vivo models
sec.p: All experiments were performed with approval from the Malmö/Lund Animal Ethics Committee, protocol nos. 16318/2019 and 18602/2023, in line with ARRIVE guidelines. Female F1 human CD40 transgenic hCD40tgxC57BL/6 (26) mice aged 8 to 12 weeks were used in the experiments.

Mice were inoculated with 0.5 × 106 MC38-CEA in PBS or 0.25 × 106 MC38-CEA in growth factor–reduced Matrigel (356252, Corning) diluted 1:1 in PBS subcutaneously in the flank and randomly divided into groups of 10. CEACAM5 expression was confirmed prior to each inoculation through flow cytometry. Tumors were measured using calipers 2 to 3 times per week following day 6 of inoculation. Tumor volume was calculated using the following formula: (width/2 × length/2 × height/2) × 4p/3. Animals were sacrificed when ethical endpoints were reached (including tumor volume exceeding 2 cm3, tumor ulceration, or affected health) or at the termination of the experiment. ED50 was defined as the dose at which 50% of the mice were cured and was calculated using GraphPad Prism 9.3.1.

For the antitumor experiments, mice were treated intraperitoneally 3 times every 3 or 4 days with ATOR-4066 or controls starting on days 6, 10, or 13. Mice treated with the PD-1 antibody (50 µg/dose, Clone RPM1-14, Bio X Cell, RRID: AB_10949053) were treated intraperitoneally starting on day 10. For T-cell depletion, mice were administered 200 µg of anti-CD4 (BE0003-1, Bio X Cell) and anti-CD8 (BE0061, Bio X Cell) depleting antibodies intraperitoneally. T-cell depletion was confirmed by flow cytometric analysis of peripheral blood 24 hours after the second antibody treatment.

For rechallenge experiments, complete responders (CR) and naïve mice were inoculated with twin tumors, with 0.5 × 106 MC38-CEA on the right flank and 1.0 × 106 MC38-WT (Kerafast, ENH204-FP) or 0.1 × 106 B16-F10 (ATCC, CRL-6475, RRID: CVCL_0159) on the left flank, in a volume of 200 µL PBS for each tumor. For T-cell depletion during rechallenge, mice were treated with 200 µg anti-CD4 (BE0003-1, Bio X Cell) and anti-CD8 (BE0061, Bio X Cell) on day 2 (in relation to the second tumor inoculation) and 100 µg anti-CD4 and anti-CD8 on days −1, 0, 4, 8, 11, and 15.

sec.title: IHC
sec.p: hCD40tgxC57BL/6 mice were inoculated with 0.5 × 106 MC38-CEA in PBS subcutaneously in the flank and treated with either ATOR-4066 (167 µg/mouse), bsAb isotype (167 µg/mouse), CD40 mAb (100 µg/mouse, equimolar to ATOR-4066 and bsAb isotype dose), or vehicle on days 6, 10, and 13 after inoculation. Tumors were dissected on day 14 and snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen. Cryosections (8 mm) were prepared from the cryopreserved tumors using a Leica Cryocut 1800 cryotome and dried at room temperature overnight, and IHC staining was performed. Tumors from all treatment groups were stained for the detection of human IgG by a rabbit anti-human IgG (3.6 µg/mL, 309-005-082, Jackson ImmunoResearch) followed by incubation with an anti-rabbit BrightVision horseradish peroxidase antibody (RRID: AB_2915958). Tumors from vehicle-treated mice were also stained for CEACAM5 using an FITC-conjugated anti-CEACAM5 (K-293-FITC) at a concentration of 4 µg/mL prepared in 5% normal mouse serum in PBS. A rabbit anti-FITC (1.3 µg/mL, RRID: AB_619423) followed by anti-rabbit BrightVision horseradish peroxidase (RRID: AB_2915958) was used for detection. Information about the materials and reagents used for IHC can be found in Supplementary Table S2. The stained sections were analyzed using a Leica DMRX/E microscope; representative images were taken, followed by histopathologic scoring.

sec.title: RNA sequencing
sec.p: hCD40tgxC57BL/6 mice were inoculated with 0.5 × 106 MC38-CEA in PBS subcutaneously in the flank. Mice were treated intraperitoneally on days 6 and 10 with ATOR-4066 (167 µg/mouse), CD40 mAb (100 µg/mouse, equimolar to the ATOR-4066 dose), or vehicle. Mice were sacrificed on day 11, and tumors, lymph nodes, and peripheral blood were collected in RNAlater (Thermo Fisher Scientific, AM7021). Tumors were analyzed either as whole tissue or the immune compartment was sorted (CD45+Ly6G–). For sorted immune cells, tumors were mechanically and enzymatically digested with 0.38 mg/mL Liberase TL (Roche) and 0.1 mg/mL DNase I (Roche) for 30 minutes at 37°C. After incubation, the samples were passed through a 70 μm cell strainer. Single-cell suspensions were stained using fluorochrome-labeled antibodies against CD45 (561037, BD Biosciences) and Ly6G (560602, BD Biosciences) and a viability stain (FVS620, 564996, BD Biosciences). A minimum of 20,000 live CD45+Ly6G– cells were sorted using a FACSAria cell sorter (BD Biosciences) into lysis buffer from the PureLink RNA Mini Kit (12183018A), and RNA was extracted as per the manufacturer’s instructions for cell suspensions. RNA isolation from whole tumors was done using the PureLink RNA Mini Kit (12183018A), following the instructions for lysing tissues with a pestle and mortar. RNA was isolated from peripheral blood using Mouse RiboPure (AM1951, Invitrogen), following the manufacturer’s instructions.

RNA concentrations were measured using Qubit Flex (Q33327, Invitrogen, Thermo Fisher Scientific), and RNA quality was measured on TapeStation 4200 (Agilent) as per the manufacturer’s instructions. mRNA library preparation was done with Illumina Stranded mRNA Prep, Ligation (20040534, Illumina) and sequenced on a NovaSeq 6000 System (20012850, Illumina) with a read length of 2 × 150 bp and 50 million reads per sample. Sequences were aligned to the Mus musculus genome (GRCm38) using STAR (v5.1) and quantified with Salmon (v1.10). Count matrices were imported to R (v4.2.2) for analysis. Gene count matrices were analyzed to remove low-expressing genes and for samples with large interindividual z-score distributions. Raw gene counts were normalized, and differentially expressed genes (DEG) between treatment conditions were analyzed using DESeq2 (v1.38.3, RRID: SCR_000154; ref. 27). Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed on z-score–normalized variance stabilization transformed gene counts using prcomp. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was done using EnrichR (v3.2; ref. 28). Gene set variation analysis (GSVA) was performed with GSVA (v1.48.3; ref. 29). Transcription factor activity was calculated using a univariate linear model with regulon information from CollecTRI using decoupleR (v2.8.0; ref. 30). Immune cell deconvolution was performed using CIBERSORTx with a custom signature matrix based on single-cell RNA sequencing of MC38 tumors (31).

sec.title: Flow cytometry of myeloid cells and T cells
sec.p: For the analysis of myeloid cell populations, tumor-inoculated mice were treated intraperitoneally on days 6 and 10 with 100 µg/mouse of CD40 mAb, 167 µg/mouse of ATOR-4066 (equimolar concentration to mAb), or vehicle. Tumors, spleen, and draining lymph nodes were isolated into ice-cold RPMI (61870-010, Gibco), and tumors were weighed on day 11 after inoculation, 24 hours after the second treatment. For the analysis of T-cell responses, mice were treated intraperitoneally on days 13, 17, and 20 with 100 µg/mouse of CD40 mAb, 167 µg/mouse of ATOR-4066, or vehicle. Tumors, lymph nodes, and spleen were isolated into ice-cold RPMI on day 21 after inoculation, 24 hours after the third treatment.

Tumors were mechanically and enzymatically digested with 0.38 mg/mL Liberase TL (Roche) and 0.1 mg/mL DNase I (Roche) for 30 minutes at 37°C. After incubation, the samples were passed through a 70 μm cell strainer before CD45+ cells were isolated by MACS sorting using CD45 microbeads (130-052-301, Miltenyi Biotec) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Spleens and lymph nodes were passed through a 70-μm cell strainer to obtain a single-cell suspension. Cells were counted using a Countess II (Invitrogen). Single-cell suspensions for all samples were stained using fluorochrome-labeled antibodies listed in Supplementary Table S1, and data were acquired using FACSymphony A1 (BD Biosciences). Data were analyzed using FlowJo (v10.10.0, RRID: SCR_008520).

sec.title: Multiplex cytokine analysis
sec.p: Mice were treated intraperitoneally on day 6 only or on days 6 and 10 with ATOR-4066 (10, 40, 167, or 360 µg/mouse), CD40 mAb (100 µg/mouse, equimolar dose to 167 µg of bsAb), or vehicle. Peripheral blood was drawn 24 hours after the last treatment (either day 7 or 11), and mice were sacrificed to collect tumors. The blood was kept at room temperature for 30 to 60 minutes before centrifugation (2,000 × g, 10 minutes) and collection of plasma for analysis. Tumors were lysed by grinding with a mortar and pestle in PBS before the addition of lysis buffer (Cell Lysis Buffer 2, R&D Systems) and incubation at room temperature for 30 minutes. The samples were centrifuged (6,000 × g, 4 minutes), and supernatants were used for analysis. Cytokine levels in the plasma and tumors were analyzed by following the instructions of the Luminex Discovery Assay kit (LXSAMSM, R&D Systems). The samples were read using a Bio-Rad analyzer with standard settings.

sec.title: Mixed lymphocyte reaction in cultures of exhausted T cells and allogenic MoDCs
sec.p: Human CD8+ T cells or CD4+ T cells were enriched from PBMC isolated from leukocyte concentrates obtained from healthy donors by negative selection using a MACS CD8+ T Cell Isolation Kit II (130-096-495, Miltenyi Biotec) or CD4+ T Cell Isolation Kit II (130-096-533, Miltenyi Biotec), respectively. Human CD8+ or CD4+ T cells with an exhausted phenotype were generated by repeated stimulation over a period of 7 days in culture with CD3/CD28 Dynabeads (1:1 beads/cell ratio, 11131D, Gibco) and recombinant human IL2 (100 IU/mL, 202-IL, R&D Systems). Every second day, for a total of 3 times during the expansion period, fresh CD3/CD28 Dynabeads were added to the T cells. After 8 days, exhausted CD8+ or CD4+ T cells were characterized as having increased expression of PD-1, TIM-3, and LAG-3 with flow cytometry (Supplementary Fig. S1A and S1B).

Human MoDCs were generated as described above (see in vitro assays). The MoDCs were then matured for 24 hours by adding IL1β, IL6, and TNFα (10 ng/mL, 130-093-563, 130-093-901, and 130-094-023, respectively, Miltenyi Biotec) and PGE2 (1 µg/mL, P0409, Merck Millipore). The flow cytometric phenotypic characterization of MoDCs is shown in Supplementary Fig. S1C. CEACAM5-coated beads were generated by incubating biotinylated recombinant human CEACAM-5/CD66e Fc chimera Avi-tag (AVI10449, R&D Systems) with Dynabeads M-280 Streptavidin (11206D, Invitrogen) for 30 minutes at room temperature.

Titrations of anti–PD-1 (nivolumab, Bristol Myers Squibb) and a set concentration of ATOR-4066, 1 nmol/L (or the reverse, titrations of ATOR-4066 and a set concentration of anti–PD-1, 100 nmol/L), and CEACAM5-coated beads (0.4 × 106 beads/mL) were used to treat a 1:10 mix of MoDC cells and exhausted CD8+ T cells or CD4+ T cells for 7 days in a mixed lymphocyte reaction (MLR) assay. Supernatants were analyzed for IFNγ using the Monkey IFNγ ELISA Development Kit (3421M-1H-20, Mabtech). IFNγ levels (background subtracted) were normalized, and dose–response curves were plotted using GraphPad Prism 9.3.1. Synergy scores were calculated using the Bliss, zero interaction potency, and highest single agent methods in the SynergyFinder R package (32).

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Statistical analysis was performed using GraphPad Prism 9.3.1 or R (v4.2.2). Group sizes were determined by considering expected variations based on previous experience. Survival analyses are presented as Kaplan–Meier curves and analyzed by the log-rank (Mantel–Cox) test. Unless otherwise stated, data are presented as the mean with SD. Paired data were analyzed using the one-sided Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed-rank test and unpaired data with the Mann–Whitney U test. For comparisons of more than two groups, one-way ANOVA with the Tukey multiple comparison tests or Kruskal–Wallis with Dunn’s multiple comparison tests were used for parametric and nonparametric data, respectively. Differences between combination treatment or mono-treatment in MLR experiments were analyzed by two-way ANOVA with repeated measures and Bonferroni correction. The PCA of cytokine levels was performed on Z-scaled concentration values. RNA sequencing data were analyzed as described above. P < 0.05 or adjusted P value (Padj) < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

sec.title: ATOR-4066 is a Neo-X-Prime bsAb that binds CD40 and CEACAM5
sec.p: ATOR-4066 was generated and designed in the bispecific tetravalent RUBY format containing a silent Fc domain (IgG1 LALA, Fig. 1A; ref. 22). The CEACAM5-binding domain was obtained from the Alligator-GOLD library, a proprietary antibody library. The CD40-binding domain, which binds to module 2 in domain 1 of CD40 (Supplementary Fig. S2), was derived from the binding domain in mitazalimab (ADC-1013; refs. 24, 25). The key aspects of the Neo-X-Prime concept and ATOR-4066 mode of action are as follows: (i) the ability to cluster tumor-derived extracellular vesicles and APCs and (ii) the ability to conditionally activate CD40-expressing cells in the presence of TAA (e.g., CEACAM5)-expressing cells (Fig. 1B) have been described previously (12). In this study, the ability of ATOR-4066 to induce CEACAM5-conditional activation of human MoDCs cocultured with a human gastric carcinoma cell line (MKN-45) was confirmed, resulting in an EC50 value of 0.26 nmol/L (Fig. 1C; Supplementary Fig. S3). As soluble CEACAM5 is present at high levels in the circulation in patients with CEACAM5-positive tumors, we ensured that the CEACAM5 binder used for ATOR-4066 provided an epitope and affinity/avidity profile (Supplementary Fig. S4), enabling high potency without interference from physiologically relevant levels of soluble CEACAM5. The results showed that the ability to activate CD40-expressing cells in the presence of soluble CEACAM5 was retained and that soluble CEACAM5 did not induce exaggerated immune activation (Fig. 1D; Supplementary Fig. S5). To demonstrate that ATOR-4066 can induce CEACAM5-conditional activation of immune cells in the context of human tumors, dissociated tumor material obtained from patients with gastric cancer was analyzed ex vivo. The results showed that ATOR-4066 stimulation induces the activation of myeloid cells, B cells, and CD4+ T cells, but not CD8+ T cells, residing in the TME of patients with gastric cancer, as measured by the upregulation of CD83 or CD25, respectively (Fig. 1E; Supplementary Table S3). Lastly, ATOR-4066 displayed favorable developability properties, as demonstrated by a production yield of >3 g/L in 2L bioreactors (Fig. 1F). In summary, ATOR-4066 displays the biophysical and biological functions required for the clinical development of a Neo-X-Prime bsAb.

B, Mode of action of ATOR-4066, as proposed by Hägerbrand and colleagues (12). Mean ± SD of normalized IL12 levels of nine donors was calculated, and EC50 values were determined. E, DTCs, including tumor-infiltrating CD40+ immune cells and CEACAM5+ tumor cells, obtained from patients with gastric cancer (n = 6), were stimulated with ATOR-4066 in vitro for 72 hours, and activation markers, CD83 on myeloid cells and B cells, and CD25 on CD4 and CD8 T cells, were assessed using flow cytometry. sec.title: ATOR-4066 induces strong antitumor activity in syngeneic MC38 tumors expressing human CEACAM5
sec.p: The antitumor activity of ATOR-4066 was investigated using subcutaneous MC38 tumors expressing human CEACAM5 (62,300 CEACAM5 molecules/cell) established in a human CD40 transgenic mouse model. Doses ranging between 10 and 167 µg/mouse, corresponding to 0.5 to 8.35 mg/kg (based on the average mouse weight of 20 g), were investigated with the administration of ATOR-4066 on days 6, 10, and 13. This established an ED50 value of approximately 3 mg/kg and a maximal antitumor activity observed at 8.35 mg/kg (Fig. 2A; Supplementary Fig. S6). We further demonstrated that maximum antitumor activity was also obtained at higher doses, as assessed up to 50 mg/kg (Supplementary Fig. S7). No systemic immune activation or increase in liver enzyme (aspartate aminotransferase, Supplementary Fig. S8) was observed at the highest tested dose level, whereas a positive control [CP-870,893/clone 21.4.1, analog to selicrelumab (33)] increased spleen and liver weight, altered cytokine levels in livers, and increased systemic levels of cytokines such as CXCL10 and IL6 (Supplementary Fig. S8). The antitumor activity at the maximal effective dose level (8.35 mg/kg, 167 µg) was compared with the activity of the corresponding monospecific CD40 antibody (CD40 mAb) at the molar equivalent dose level, and it was demonstrated that ATOR-4066 had superior antitumor activity in this CEACAM5-positive tumor model system (Fig. 2B; Supplementary Fig. S9A).

caption.p: ATOR-4066 demonstrates strong antitumor activity in syngeneic MC38-expressing human CEACAM5. A, The dose-dependent response of ATOR-4066 was studied in F1 hCD40tgxC57BL/6 mice inoculated with MC38-CEA and treated with the indicated dose of ATOR-4066 or vehicle 6, 10, and 13 days after inoculation, n = 10–27. B, The antitumor effect of ATOR-4066 was compared with an equimolar dose of CD40 mAb and vehicle. C, Flow cytometry analysis and IHC were used to determine CEACAM5 expression in tumors at the indicated time points after cell inoculation in untreated mice, n = 6–10. D, The IHC score was used to determine antibody accumulation in mice treated with 167 μg ATOR-4066, 100 μg of CD40 mAb IHC, or isotype control. Bars represent mean ± SD; each point represents one mouse; n = 5. E and F, Kaplan–Meier plots of mice in which ATOR-4066 treatment (167 µg/dose) was started either 10 days after inoculation (E) or 13 days after inoculation (F); n = 20. Data represent a representative experiment (from two independent experiments) performed (B and D) or pooled data from two (C, E, F) independent experiments performed. *, P ≤ 0.05; **, P ≤ 0.01; ***, P ≤ 0.001; ****, P ≤ 0.0001. MFI, mean fluorescence intensity.

sec.p: The expression of CEACAM5 in inoculated MC38-CEA tumors was analyzed by flow cytometry at multiple time points, demonstrating a significant reduction in both the percentage of CEACAM5-positive cells and the expression levels of CEACAM5 over time (Fig. 2C). IHC analysis of tumors 14 days after inoculation confirmed heterogeneous CEACAM5 expression in the established tumors (Fig. 2C; Supplementary Fig. S10). Next, the target occupancy was assessed by IHC of tumors 24 hours after two treatments (days 10 and 13), and this showed a significantly larger accumulation of ATOR-4066 in CEACAM5-expressing tumors compared with both a CD40 mAb and an isotype bsAb control (Fig. 2D).

The antitumor activity of ATOR-4066 in larger tumors with more heterogeneous CEACAM5 expression was evaluated by delaying treatment start to days 10 or 13. ATOR-4066 treatment (167 µg/dose) starting 10 days (tumor mean size 260 mm3; range 59–620 mm3) after tumor inoculation cured all mice (Fig. 2E; Supplementary Fig. S9B), including mice with large tumors (>600 mm3), despite the fact that approximately 30% of the tumor cells were CEACAM5-negative (Fig. 2C). Treatment with 167 µg/dose ATOR-4066 starting on day 13 (tumor mean size 280 mm3; range 76–900 mm3) also resulted in significant antitumor activity, curing 9 of 19 mice (Fig. 2F; Supplementary Fig. S9C). Together, these data demonstrate that ATOR-4066 can cure mice with well-established tumors with heterogeneous CEACAM5 expression.

sec.title: Pharmacodynamic responses to ATOR-4066 in blood and tumors as measured by RNA sequencing
sec.p: To identify pharmacodynamic effects of ATOR-4066 that correlate with its superior antitumor efficacy compared with CD40 mAb, we performed bulk RNA sequencing of peripheral blood, whole tumors, and the immune compartment of the tumor (A). PCA of the transcriptomic profiles in the tumor revealed clustering of tumors treated with ATOR-4066, distinctly separated from vehicle and CD40 mAb (Fig. 3B). GSEA of the genes driving the main separation between vehicle and ATOR-4066 revealed an enrichment of gene pathways related to inflammatory response and cytokine-mediated signaling pathways (Supplementary Fig. S11). Additionally, the separation along PC1 (explaining 70.8% of the variance) in the PCA of peripheral blood showed that ATOR-4066 elicited substantially lower peripheral transcriptomic alterations than the CD40 mAb (Fig. 3C).

caption.p: ATOR-4066 alters the transcription profiles of tumors and intratumoral immune cells to a proinflammatory state. A, Transcriptomic alterations induced by ATOR-4066 in blood, tumors, and intratumoral immune cells were studied in F1 hCD40tgxC57BL/6 mice inoculated with MC38-CEACAM5 tumor cells. B and C, PCA illustrated large transcriptomic changes in tumors but not in peripheral blood following ATOR-4066 treatment. D, Gene expression profiles of all DEGs in tumors between the treatment conditions were clustered, and GSEA was performed on each gene cluster. E, GSVA was performed on the top enriched and CD40-related pathways. F, Gene expression of selected canonical inflammatory or immune activation genes. G, The activity of transcription factors (TF) was estimated, and the activity of the top varying transcription factors is shown. H, Gene expression profiles of all DEGs in intratumoral immune cells between the treatment conditions were clustered, and GSEA was performed on each gene cluster. I and J, Immune cell composition was estimated based on CIBERSORTx, and canonical genes for cell populations of immune activation were analyzed. *, P ≤ 0.05; **, P ≤ 0.01. NA, not applicable; Pos., positive; Reg., regulation; VST, variance stabilization transformed.

sec.p: To further evaluate the intratumoral pharmacodynamic effects of ATOR-4066, we investigated DEGs between each treatment group (Supplementary Fig. S11). The DEGs were subsequently clustered based on their expression, which identified four gene clusters (Fig. 3D). Enrichment analysis of the genes that were part of the gene cluster with upregulated DEGs following both ATOR-4066 and CD40 mAb treatment indicated that these genes were mainly involved in the positive regulation of chemotaxis and leukocyte migration. One cluster of genes that were solely upregulated in tumors of ATOR-4066–treated mice was seen to be related to inflammatory response and cytokine-mediated signaling. Furthermore, GSVA showed an increased expression of genes related to inflammatory responses, cytokine production, and immune cell recruitment in tumors of ATOR-4066–treated mice (Fig. 3E). These findings were supported by a higher expression of genes related to inflammation (such as Il-1β and Il-6), immune activation (such as Cd80 and Cd274), and immune migration (such as Icam1) in tumors of ATOR-4066–treated mice (Fig. 3F). Moreover, GSVA showed an increased expression of genes related to macrophages, neutrophils, DC chemotaxis, and antigen presentation, as well as T-cell proliferation (Fig. 3E). Lastly, the analysis of transcription factor activity showed an increased activity of transcription factors related to immune activation (such as NF-κB, Stat1, and Irf1) and immune cell differentiation (Spi1) in tumors of ATOR-4066–treated mice (Fig. 3G). In contrast, untreated mice were characterized by an increased activation of E2f1 and E2f4, transcription factors associated with the cell cycle and colorectal cancer.

We then analyzed the transcriptomic alterations induced by ATOR-4066 treatment on the immune cells (CD45+Ly6G–) within the TME. By performing similar differential gene expression analysis and clustering of gene expression as aforementioned, we identified a set of genes that were only upregulated following ATOR-4066 treatment. Enrichment analysis implied that these genes were related to cell proliferation and T-cell activation (Fig. 3H). We next used CIBERSORTx, with a signature matrix from previously defined immune populations in MC38, to estimate the immune cell proportions. This showed a relative increase in DCs [both conventional DC 1 (cDC1) and cDC2] as well as CD4+ T cells in ATOR-4066–treated mice compared with both vehicle- and CD40 mAb–treated mice (Fig. 3I; Supplementary Fig. S11). The increase in T cells was also seen by an increase in canonical T-cell genes such as Cd3e, Cd4, and Cd8a, as well as genes related to T-cell activation such as Cd28 and Pdcd1 (Fig. 3J). Lastly, increased expression Mki-67 and Cd80 further supported that ATOR-4066 treatment drives immune cell proliferation and activation (Fig. 3J).

sec.title: ATOR-4066 induces activation and increase in myeloid cells in the TME
sec.p: We next explored the effects of ATOR-4066 on the myeloid cell populations within the TME. Tumor-bearing mice were treated with either ATOR-4066 (167 µg/dose) or an equimolar amount of CD40 mAbs (on days 6 and 10), and the tumors were analyzed by flow cytometry 24 hours after the last treatment (Fig. 4A). We observed that ATOR-4066 induced a significant increase in immune cells within the TME (Fig. 4B). Moreover, t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding analysis identified a separation of myeloid cell populations and revealed distinct treatment effects on monocyte and macrophage populations with ATOR-4066 but not with CD40 mAbs (Fig. 4C). A significant increase in monocytes was observed following treatment with ATOR-4066 (Fig. 4D). Moreover, ATOR-4066 increased the proportion of activated monocytes within the TME, as indicated by the significantly higher percentage of monocytes expressing CD86 or PD-L1 in ATOR-4066–treated samples (Fig. 4D; Supplementary Fig. S12). Although there was no treatment effect on the intratumoral macrophage or DC densities, a significant increase in both the proportion of activated macrophages and DCs was observed with ATOR-4066 treatment (Fig. 4E and F).

A, F1 hCD40tgxC57BL/6 mice were inoculated with MC38-CEA and treated with 167 μg of ATOR-4066, 100 μg (equimolar dose) of CD40 mAb, or vehicle 6 and 10 days after inoculation. Tumors were isolated 11 days after inoculation, dissociated, stained using fluorescently labeled antibodies, and analyzed using flow cytometry. B, CD45+ density (cell/mg tumor). C, t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding (t-SNE) visualization of macrophages, neutrophils, monocytes, and DC populations. D–F, Cell density of monocytes, macrophages, and DCs in tumors enumerated and expression of CD86 and PD-L1 in corresponding populations. G, Data represent pooled data from two independent experiments performed with similar results, n = 8–10. Proportion of neutrophils among immune cells and neutrophil tumor density (cells/mg tumor) were enumerated. H, Enrichment of gene expression of genes related to neutrophil-mediated immunity (Gene Ontology: 0002446) was quantified by GSEA. I and J, Gene expression and cytokine levels of neutrophil-related functions were analyzed. Bars represent the mean and SD. Each dot represents one mouse. Data represent a representative experiment (from two independent experiments) performed. *, P ≤ 0.05; **, P ≤ 0.01. NES, normalized enrichment score.

sec.p: A significant increase in the intratumoral neutrophil population, both in cell density and proportion of CD45+ cells, was observed following ATOR-4066 treatment (Fig. 4G). This finding was further supported by RNA sequencing results, from which GSEA suggested a significant increase in neutrophil-mediated immunity (Fig. 4H) and a significant increase in the expression of the canonical neutrophil gene Ly6g and the neutrophil-related gene S100a9 (Fig. 4I). Lastly, a significantly increased amount of S100A9 was detected in tumor lysates from mice treated with ATOR-4066 (Fig. 4J).

Myeloid cell activation was detected in the spleen following ATOR-4066 treatment; however, it was significantly lower than what was observed in the CD40 mAb–treated cohort. No myeloid cell activation was observed in lymph nodes in ATOR-4066–treated mice (Supplementary Fig. S13).

sec.title: Treatment with ATOR-4066 results in upregulation of proinflammatory cytokines in the TME but not in the periphery
sec.p: Next, we investigated the effects of ATOR-4066 treatment on cytokine activity. By analyzing the expression of all genes related to cytokine activity (Gene Ontology: 0005125), we observed that ATOR-4066 induced distinct alterations in cytokine expression, which included upregulation of several proinflammatory cytokines such as Ccl3, Ccl4, Ccl5, TNF, and IL1b (Supplementary Fig. S14). To evaluate if these changes translated into changes in intratumoral cytokine levels, we performed a 22-plex cytokine analysis of tumor lysates. First, the effects of one treatment (6 days after tumor inoculation) of either ATOR-4066 or CD40 mAb were measured 24 hours after treatment (Fig. 5A). In total, 19 cytokines were detected in the tumor lysates (Supplementary Fig. S14) and analyzed by PCA. A dose-dependent shift along PC1 (explaining 50.6% of the variance) was observed for ATOR-4066–treated samples. The PCA loadings revealed that the main drivers for separation between higher ATOR-4066 doses (167 and 360 µg) and controls were TNFα, CCL4, CXCL1, IL1α, IL1β, ICAM-1, IL6, and CCL11 (Fig. 5B). Individual analysis of the concentration of these cytokines showed a dose-dependent increase with ATOR-4066 treatment (Fig. 5C). Moreover, a comparison of treatment using the equimolar dose of ATOR-4066 and a CD40 mAb (167 and 100 µg/mouse, respectively) demonstrated a significantly higher concentration of all of these cytokines, except for CXCL1, in ATOR-4066–treated tumor lysates (Fig. 5D). No significant increases in cytokine levels were detected in the circulation following treatment with ATOR-4066. However, systemic increases in cytokines following CD40 mAb treatment were observed (Fig. 5D).

caption.p: ATOR-4066 increases levels of proinflammatory cytokines in tumors but not in the circulation. A and E, Cytokine levels were determined in plasma and tumor homogenate using Luminex analysis in F1 hCD40tgxC57BL/6 mice inoculated with MC38-CEA and treated with 10, 40, 167, or 360 µg of ATOR-4066, 100 μg (equimolar dose to 167 µg of ATOR-4066) of CD40 mAbs, or vehicle 6 and 10 days after cell inoculation. Tumors and plasma were isolated 7 or 11 days after inoculation, n = 5. Data represent a representative experiment (from two independent experiments) performed. B and F, PCA was used to determine main separators in tumor lysates between treatment groups. Dots represent individual mice, and arrows show PC loadings. C and G, Dose–response curves of the effect of ATOR-4066 on intratumoral cytokine levels of the cytokines identified as main separators. Thick lines represent the mean, and shadowed areas represent SD. D and H, Concentration of cytokines in tumors and blood following treatment with equimolar doses of ATOR-4066 and CD40 mAbs (167 and 100 µg, respectively). The bar graph shows the mean with SD. Dots show individual mice (n = 5), and missing dots indicate that cytokine levels were below the limit of detection. *, P ≤ 0.05; **, P ≤ 0.01.

sec.p: We conducted a similar cytokine analysis 11 days after inoculation after two treatments with ATOR-4066 or CD40 mAbs (Fig. 5E). PCA of cytokine levels in tumors showed distinct separation between mice treated with higher doses of ATOR-4066 (167 and 360 µg/dose) and vehicle, CD40 mAb treatment, and lower doses of ATOR-4066. Moreover, the top PCA loadings showed that the separation along PC1 (explaining 43.5% of the variance) was mainly driven by a higher concentration of IL10, IL1β, CXCL2, ICAM-1, S100A9, and IL33 but a lower concentration of CXCL10 and CCL2 in ATOR-4066–treated mice (Fig. 5F). When analyzed individually, the cytokines driving positive separation in PC1 had a dose-dependent increase in concentration with ATOR-4066 treatment. However, the concentrations of CCL2 and CXCL10 were reduced with higher concentrations of ATOR-4066 (Fig. 5G). Contrary to the tumors, there were no systemic alterations of the cytokines following two treatments of ATOR-4066 (Fig. 5H; Supplementary Fig. S15).

sec.title: T cell–independent mechanisms initially control tumor growth, but long-term tumor control depends on T cells
sec.p: To investigate the role of T cells in tumor rejection following ATOR-4066 treatment, we administered ATOR-4066 to tumor-bearing mice that were either depleted of T cells or not (Supplementary Fig. S16). There was a significant early reduction in tumor growth in mice treated with ATOR-4066, with or without T-cell depletion, compared with vehicle control. However, mice that were not depleted of T cells had sustained long-term tumor control and survival benefits following ATOR-4066 treatment, whereas tumor growth in the T cell–depleted cohort recurred about 20 days after tumor inoculation (Fig. 6A), demonstrating a critical role of ATOR-4066 treatment–activated T cells in the response.

caption.p: T cells are critical for the antitumor effect generated by ATOR-4066. A, The importance of T cells during treatment was evaluated using aCD4- and aCD8-depleting antibodies in F1 hCD40tgxC57BL/6 mice inoculated with MC38-CEA and treated with ATOR-4066 or vehicle 6, 10, and 13 days after tumor inoculation. Tumor volume was measured, and survival was recorded. B, To analyze T-cell infiltration and activation, flow cytometry analysis was performed on tumor tissue after three treatments starting on day 13. C and D, T-cell frequency of immune cells and tumor density (cell/mg tumor) were determined, as well as CD4 and CD8 tumor cell density and frequency of expression of GrB, Ki-67, and PD-1 in corresponding populations. E, To study immunologic memory in mice cured of MC38-CEA tumors by ATOR-4066 treatment, mice were rechallenged with MC38-CEA and MC38-wt or MC38-CEA and B16 on opposite sides of the flank. Tumor volumes were measured. Cured: cured the indicated tumor, volume = 0 mm3 at the experiment endpoint; bars represent mean ± SD. F, The importance of memory T cells in rechallenge was investigated using aCD4- and aCD8-depleting antibodies as indicated. T cells in mice were depleted around rechallenge, and tumor volume and survival were recorded. A and F, Dots and lines represent the mean ± SEM. E, Each line represents one mouse. A and F, Data represent a representative experiment (from two independent experiments) performed. C–E, Pooled data from two independent experiments were performed. *, P ≤ 0.05; **, P ≤ 0.01; ***, P ≤ 0.001; ****, P ≤ 0.0001.

sec.p: Changes in intratumoral T cells were investigated using flow cytometry, which demonstrated a significant increase in both T-cell density and the proportion of T cells in ATOR-4066–treated animals compared with both vehicle- and CD40 mAb–treated mice (Fig. 6B and C). Although the CD8+ T–cell density was not significantly increased in ATOR-4066–treated animals, the proportion of CD8+ T cells that were positive for granzyme B or PD-1 was significantly increased compared with vehicle or both vehicle and CD40 mAbs, respectively (Fig. 6D). Moreover, the intratumoral CD4+ T-cell density in ATOR-4066–treated mice was significantly higher compared with both vehicle and CD40 mAb treatment. Lastly, the fraction of CD4+ T cells that were positive for either granzyme B, PD-1, or Ki-67 was significantly higher in ATOR-4066–treated animals compared with controls (Fig. 6D). Although no differences in the number of either CD4+ or CD8+ T cells were observed in the spleen or lymph node between the cohorts of mice, some activation was observed in the corresponding populations in ATOR-4066–treated mice compared with the vehicle-treated group (Supplementary Fig. S17). However, in most cases, the percentages of PD-1, Ki-67, and granzyme B were significantly lower in the T-cell populations in the spleen and lymph node of ATOR-4066–treated mice compared with CD40 mAb–treated mice.

To assess whether ATOR-4066 treatment induced immunologic memory against MC38 tumor antigens, naïve mice or mice that had previously been cured of MC38-CEA tumors by ATOR-4066 (CR mice) were inoculated with MC38-CEA and MC38-WT or MC38-CEA and B16.F10 tumor cells on opposite flanks (Fig. 6E). All except one of the CR mice, but not the naïve mice, rejected MC38-CEA tumors, indicating immunologic memory following ATOR-4066 treatment. Moreover, 9 of 19 CR mice rejected MC38-WT tumors, whereas no naïve mice did, suggesting that ATOR-4066 treatment induced immunologic memory to tumor antigens other than CEACAM5. Furthermore, inoculation with irrelevant tumor cells (B16.F10 cells) showed that the memory was specific to MC38, as B16.F10 tumors grew in CR mice, whereas MC38-CEA tumors did not (Fig. 6E; Supplementary Fig. S16). Next, we confirmed that the immunologic memory toward MC38-CEA tumors was T cell–dependent, as tumors grew in CR mice depleted of T cells (Fig. 6F).

sec.title: Combination with PD-1 results in the synergistic activation of T cells in vitro and enhanced antitumor activity of ATOR-4066
sec.p: The functional effects of combining ATOR-4066 and anti–PD-1 treatment were assessed in an in vitro model mixing exhausted primary human CD4+ or CD8+ T cells with allogenic MoDCs (Fig. 7A; Supplementary Fig. S18). A synergistic effect on the activation of exhausted CD8+ T cells, as measured by Bliss, zero interaction potency, and highest single-agent synergy scores, was observed at concentrations above 0.6 nmol/L ATOR-4066 in combination with PD-1 inhibition. For CD4+ T cells, the combination effect was additive at the tested concentrations (Fig. 7A and B; Supplementary Fig. S19).

caption.p: ATOR-4066 in combination with the PD-1 inhibitor enhances the activation of exhausted T cells and controls tumor growth. A and B, ATOR-4066 was evaluated in combination with the anti–PD-1 antibody Opdivo in MLR assays using allogeneic exhausted human primary CD4+ or CD8+ T cells and mature MoDCs. CD4+ or CD8+ T cells with an exhausted phenotype were expanded for 7 days with Dynabeads and then rested overnight in medium. Titrations of either ATOR-4066 and a constant concentration of anti–PD-1 or titrations of anti–PD-1 and a constant concentration of ATOR-4066 in the presence of CEACAM5 beads for cross-linking were used in cultures with a 1:10 mix of mature MoDC cells and exhausted T cells for 7 days before cell culture supernatants were harvested for analyzing IFNγ levels by ELISA. A, Dose–response curves (normalized data, background subtracted, and mean and SD from 9, 14, and 11 donors) are displayed. B, T-cell activation of exhausted CD8 T cells was higher for the combination of ATOR-4066 and PD-1 compared with the sum of the monospecific activity at higher concentrations, exemplified at 1 nmol/L ATOR-4066 and 100 nmol/L anti–PD-1. C and D, To study the in vivo combination treatment effect, F1 hCD40tgxC57BL/6 mice were inoculated with MC38-CEA and treated with 50 μg anti–PD-1 on days 10 and 13 after inoculation and/or 60 μg ATOR-4066 on days 6, 10, and 13 after inoculation. Survival was recorded, and tumor volume was measured. Data represent pooled data from two experiments independently performed. n = 18–20/group. conc., concentration.

sec.p: Furthermore, the antitumor effect following ATOR-4066 treatment in combination with anti–PD-1 treatment was assessed in mice inoculated with MC38-CEA cells (Fig. 7C and D). Dose levels at median effective dose (ED50) selected for the combination study (Fig. 2A; Supplementary Fig. S20), as the maximally effective dose of ATOR-4066 cures all mice, precluded the assessment of combinatorial effects. At the tested doses, the combination treatment showed a trend toward a superior effect (Fig. 7C and at a higher PD-1 dose in Supplementary Fig. S21). Although the difference in overall survival was not significant, the number of CRs (11/18 with combination vs. 6/19 with ATOR-4066 and 1/20 with anti–PD-1 treatment) was numerically higher, suggesting that the combination has the potential to improve long-lasting immune responses.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this study, we have described the characteristics of ATOR-4066, a bsAb that targets CD40 and CEACAM5. We demonstrated that ATOR-4066 has good manufacturing properties and induces CEACAM5-conditional activation of CD40-expressing APCs that drives immune activation in primary human samples. ATOR-4066 showed superior antitumor activity compared with CD40 mAbs in a CEACAM5-positive tumor model and cured mice with well-established tumors with heterogeneous CEACAM5 expression. Investigation of the intratumoral transcriptome, cytokine milieu, and immune cell profile revealed that ATOR-4066 induced myeloid cell activation, resulting in immune cell recruitment and T-cell activation. We further showed that the long-term tumor control of ATOR-4066 depends on T cells and that ATOR-4066 induces a specific T cell–dependent memory toward relevant tumor cells. Lastly, we demonstrated that ATOR-4066 synergizes with PD-1 blockade in vitro.

The design of bispecific Neo-X-Prime antibodies is important, as the format and binders determine both the functionality and developability of the antibody. ATOR-4066 was designed in the tetravalent RUBY format with two mutations (LALA) in the IgG1 Fc domain that reduce the binding to FcγR (22). Reduced binding to FcγR is important to limit activation in the absence of CEACAM5 binding, and the limited immune activation observed in the periphery supports this design. The CD40-binding domain of ATOR-4066 has been shown to be active, safe, and nonimmunogenic in clinical studies as a bivalent IgG1 WT antibody (11, 18) and was selected based on its ability to mediate strong, conditional, agonistic activity. The bivalent binding to CEACAM5 allows ATOR-4066 to bind strongly to CEACAM5-expressing cells through avidity while minimizing binding to soluble, monomeric CEACAM5 by selecting a binder with a fast dissociation rate. Maintaining functional activity, neither reducing nor exaggerating functional activity, in the presence of soluble CEACAM5 is critical for clinical development, as soluble CEACAM5 can be found at high serum levels in CEACAM5-positive patients with cancer (13). Moreover, our results show that ATOR-4066 has favorable developability properties, exemplified by the high titer from stably transfected CHO cells.

We used an hCD40tg mouse model, first described by Mangsbo and colleagues (25), to assess the antitumor activity and pharmacodynamic events in vivo. This model expresses human CD40 (no murine CD40), and as the murine CD40L can interact with human CD40, the model recaptures an intact immune system. The expression pattern of human CD40 in the hCD40tg mice is similar to mouse CD40 expression in WT mice, with some differences observed in myeloid cells (higher in hCD40tg vs. WT mice) and B cells (lower in hCD40tg mice vs. WT mice). Moreover, the MC38-CEACAM5 tumor model used in this study expresses approximately 62,300 CEACAM5 molecules per cell, which is the range observed in human tumor cell lines and represents levels expected in human tumor cells (12). However, there is no mouse homologue of CEACAM5, and thus, the only CEACAM5 present in the model system comes from the MC38-CEACAM5 tumor cells, which is a limitation of the model system. Nevertheless, the biodistribution of ATOR-4066, as previously reported when assessing a surrogate ATOR-4066 molecule in nonhuman primates (12, 22), is in line with what has been observed for the corresponding monospecific CD40 agonist (mitazalimab), displaying CD40-driven target-mediated drug disposition (11, 18). Thus, this suggests that CEACAM5 expression in normal tissue does not substantially affect the biodistribution or pharmacokinetics of ATOR-4066.

We show that ATOR-4066 treatment induces superior antitumor activity compared with monospecific CD40 treatment, with maximal antitumor activity at approximately 8 mg/kg, similar to what has been reported for other CD40 bsAbs (12, 34). Notably, we demonstrate strong antitumor activity also in large, well-established tumors with moderate and heterogeneous CEACAM5 expression. This is important as the heterogeneous expression pattern reflects the CEACAM5 expression pattern in many human cancers (35). Moreover, these data contrast ATOR-4066 with CEACAM5-targeting CD3 bsAbs and ADCs that mainly kill CEACAM5-positive cells but have a more limited capacity to induce broad antitumor immunity (35). This suggests that ATOR-4066 may be an attractive alternative or complement to ADCs and T-cell engagers in cancers with heterogeneous CEACAM5 expression.

Monoclonal CD40 therapy has been shown to induce peripheral transcriptomic alterations related to immune activation in patients with cancer (36). Here, we demonstrate that a CD40 mAb induces similar alterations to the peripheral transcriptome in our model system, whereas ATOR-4066 did not. Instead, the immune activation induced by ATOR-4066 was mainly restricted to the TME. These data both validate the relevance of our model system and support the tumor-directed and CEACAM5-conditional CD40 activation of ATOR-4066. This was further supported by the cytokine analysis that showed a distinct shift to a more proinflammatory intratumoral milieu following ATOR-4066 treatment but with limited peripheral effects on cytokine levels. Moreover, flow cytometric analysis showed that ATOR-4066 modulates the myeloid cell compartment within the TME to a more activated state, whereas limited myeloid cell activation was observed in the periphery. Furthermore, limited systemic immune activation was observed at high dose levels of ATOR-4066. We have previously, in an exploratory study in nonhuman primates, reported that a surrogate ATOR-4066 molecule is well tolerated, with no adverse findings or treatment-related changes in cytokine levels or liver enzymes (12). Together, this supports a good tolerability profile of ATOR-4066.

RNA sequencing of tumors showed that ATOR-4066 induced the expression of gene pathways such as inflammatory response, activation of macrophages and DCs, increased cytokine production, and increased leukocyte chemotaxis. These findings were subsequently confirmed with cytokine analysis and/or flow cytometry and represent known CD40 biology (3, 6). Thus, the data support the mode of action of ATOR-4066, demonstrating that it promotes a proinflammatory TME. Additionally, we saw an increase in neutrophil activity with RNA sequencing, cytokine analysis, and flow cytometry, suggesting a potential role of neutrophils in the early tumor response, as also observed by others in patients with colorectal cancer (37). Moreover, we noted a distinct increase in the alarmin cytokine IL33 in tumors after ATOR-4066 treatment, which has been shown to activate and induce the immunogenicity of cDC, as well as to induce the formation of tertiary lymphoid structures and improve prognosis in mouse models of pancreatic ductal carcinoma (38).

The activation of myeloid cells and the strong initial T cell–independent antitumor response observed suggest an important role for the innate immune system in controlling tumor growth in the early response following treatment with ATOR-4066. Our data suggest that activated myeloid cells, including activated neutrophils, are the main contributors to the T cell–independent antitumor activity, which is in line with previous studies (10, 39). Although no significant activation of NK cells was observed in the TME, we cannot rule out that they also contribute to some degree to the antitumor activity. However, it is apparent that a tumor-specific T-cell response is critical for long-term tumor control and for the development of immunologic memory to tumors following treatment with ATOR-4066. A large proportion of MC38-WT tumors were rejected in mice that had been cured of MC38-CEA tumors by ATOR-4066, suggesting that ATOR-4066 generates a broad antitumor immunity. The fact that not all CR mice rejected MC38-WT tumors is likely due to T-cell response being dominated by CEACAM5-specific T cells, as CEACAM5 is a human protein and thus foreign to mice, which makes it highly immunogenic. Importantly, the irrelevant tumor B16.F10 was not rejected by CR mice, showing that the T-cell memory was specific to tumor antigens from the original MC38 tumor. Taken together, the data suggest that ATOR-4066 acts in two steps: first, by activating tumoricidal myeloid cells that kill the tumor, and second, by activating tumor-specific T cells that then control and eradicate the tumor.

ATOR-4066 activates T cells indirectly via the activation of APCs such as DCs. It has been shown that CD40 stimulation of APCs licenses these cells to activate CD8+ T cells, bypassing the need for CD40L stimulation of APCs through CD4+ helper T cells (3, 40). However, both CD4+ and CD8+ T cells are likely important for the activity of the CD40 agonist, as shown preclinically (41, 42) and clinically, in which the role of CD4+ effector T cells has recently been highlighted (43). Furthermore, previous studies with CD40xCEACAM5 bsAbs and other CD40xTAA antibodies (12, 44) suggest that cross-priming of CD8+ T cells and direct cell–cell interactions are important for the function of this class of bsAbs. The mechanism behind the antitumor T-cell activity observed in this study likely includes both cross-priming, involving the formation of effective immune synapses between CD8+ T cells and APCs, and immune activity regulated by the observed induction of cytokines and chemokines by activated myeloid cells and CD4+ and CD8+ T cells. Further studies, potentially including the depletion of individual T-cell populations, are required to fully elucidate the respective roles of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in the antitumor effects observed with ATOR-4066.

Although ATOR-4066 displays strong antitumor activity, the mode of action and expected benign safety profile make development in combination with other treatment modalities an attractive proposition. The effects on tumor-specific T cells highlight the opportunity of using ATOR-4066 to both increase response rates in indications in which ICI therapies are approved but have limited activity, as well as to expand the scope of eligible immunotherapy indications by making tumors more T-cell inflamed (6, 7). This was supported by the MLR data, demonstrating synergistic effects when combining ATOR-4066 with a PD-1 inhibitor. Furthermore, the in vivo data showed a trend toward superior effects for the combination. However, combinations of maximally effective dose levels could not be assessed in this study, as the single-agent effect of ATOR-4066 cured all mice in this model system, which limits the interpretation of the combination effects in vivo. In addition, recent phase II data using the second-generation CD40 agonist mitazalimab in combination with modified FOLFIRINOX in pancreatic cancer demonstrated an unprecedented duration of response and prolonged overall survival, making the combination of ATOR-4066 with chemotherapy another promising clinical development route (11).

In conclusion, ATOR-4066 induces strong antitumor activity and displays the biophysical and biological activity required to activate myeloid cells through the CEACAM5-conditional activation of CD40 in human tumors, potentially also in tumors with heterogeneous CEACAM5 expression. Our data support further development and clinical testing of ATOR-4066, potentially in combination with ICI or chemotherapy.
